title: DI Fundamentals & Dagger
scopeHtml: Why DI exists, manual DI vs service locator, and Dagger's core model: components, modules, scopes, qualifiers, multibindings, assisted injection, codegen and build cost. Hilt specifics are in the Hilt chunk; Koin and alternatives in the Koin chunk.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does dependency injection solve, and how does it relate to inversion of control?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand DI as a design principle (who owns construction) rather than "a library with annotations".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A class should declare what it needs and not decide how to build it. Instead of val engine = Engine() inside Car, Car takes an Engine in its constructor and someone else wires it. That is inversion of control: the object's creation is controlled by the caller or a composition root, not by the object. The payoff is swappable implementations, testing with fakes, and dependencies visible in the API.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three ways a class gets a collaborator: it constructs it, it pulls it from a global (service locator, getSystemService), or it is handed it. Only the third is DI. Construction inside the class couples it to one concrete type, makes the real implementation run in every test, and hides the dependency from readers.

Without DI:  Car --new--> Engine          (Car owns construction, concrete coupling)
With DI:     main/composition root --> Engine --> Car(engine)
                                  Car depends on abstraction `Engine`

DI is not the same as a DI framework. Manual DI is DI. A framework only automates the wiring (the graph) and the lifetime management (scopes). Frameworks start paying off when the object graph is deep and when you need objects living for a flow rather than a whole app.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: hard dependency, untestable without real network
class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val repo = AuthRepository(OkHttpClient())
}

// DI: dependency is part of the API
class LoginViewModel(private val repo: AuthRepository) : ViewModel()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating DI with Dagger/Hilt; saying "DI means annotations".
  • Injecting everything including simple values and pure functions; DI is for collaborators with behavior.
  • Injecting Context everywhere instead of the narrow thing needed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a singleton object DI? → No, callers pull it; it is global state with hidden coupling.
  2. DI vs the Dependency Inversion principle? → DIP says depend on abstractions; DI is a technique for supplying them. Related, not identical.
  3. When is a DI framework not worth it? → Small app, shallow graph, one or two scopes; manual DI with a container class is enough.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Dagger gives us objects and helps testing." Senior: frames it as ownership of construction and lifetime, separates the principle from the tool, and chooses the tool by graph depth, scopes and team size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams with object Api singletons could not swap a backend in instrumented tests and ended up with mock web servers everywhere; constructor injection fixed it cheaply.

questions.promptHtml: Constructor, field and method injection: when do you use each, and why does Android force field injection on you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know why @Inject lateinit var exists and its costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Constructor injection is the default: immutable, fully initialized object, trivially testable with no framework. Field injection is for classes the OS instantiates (Activity, Fragment, Service) where we do not control the constructor. Method injection is rare; it is for dependencies that need this of the object after construction.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Constructor injection makes the object valid at creation time (val fields, no null window) and lets tests call the constructor directly. Field injection requires a visible lateinit var (not private, Dagger needs access) and a call like component.inject(this) at the right lifecycle moment (before super.onCreate in Activities so fragment restoration after process death finds the fields set). Hilt hides the call via generated base classes but it is the same mechanism.

Dagger also supports @Inject on methods: called after fields are injected, useful when a dependency needs the fully constructed object (for example registering this with a bus). Overusing it creates temporal coupling.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics   // field: OS creates the Activity

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        (application as MyApp).appComponent.inject(this) // before super
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    }
}

class SyncUseCase @Inject constructor(   // constructor: we own creation
    private val repo: SyncRepository
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Injecting after super.onCreate: fragments restored by the FragmentManager run before fields exist, crash with UninitializedPropertyAccessException.
  • private lateinit var with @Inject: Dagger error "Dagger does not support injection into private fields".
  • Using field injection in plain classes just out of habit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not constructor injection for Fragments? → FragmentFactory makes it possible, but it requires wiring; many teams still use field injection or Hilt.
  2. How do you inject into a ViewModel? → Constructor with @Inject plus a factory (Hilt does this with @HiltViewModel).
  3. What happens with field injection on a base class? → Dagger injects superclass members too; each class needs members-injection method for the concrete type.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists the three types. Senior: explains the lifecycle ordering bug, immutability, and that field injection is a framework concession, not a preference.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster after process death traced to an Activity calling inject() after super.onCreate, so a restored fragment read an uninitialized field.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between dependency injection and a service locator, and why does Google steer people toward DI?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The classic "is Koin DI?" debate starts here. They want the structural argument, not slogans.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With DI, the app pushes dependencies into a class from outside. With a service locator, the class pulls what it needs from a registry. The locator hides dependencies inside the implementation, makes them runtime failures, and tends to be global, which hurts tests and scoping. DI exposes them in the constructor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per Android's own guidance, the service locator is simple to start with and is a valid alternative, but: all tests share one global locator, dependencies are encoded in the implementation rather than the API surface (so a missing registration is a runtime/test failure, not a compile failure), and lifetimes other than app-wide are harder to manage.

DI:      composition root ---> [A(b, c)]      A's constructor lists needs
Locator: A() { b = Locator.get<B>() }          A's needs are invisible

Nuance: a framework like Koin can be used as DI (constructor injection only, get() only in the module definitions) or as a locator (by inject() inside classes). The pattern of use matters more than the library; but Koin resolves at runtime, so missing bindings fail at runtime unless you verify the graph in tests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Locator style: needs hidden
class Checkout {
    private val pay = ServiceLocator.paymentGateway()
}
// DI style: needs visible and replaceable
class Checkout(private val pay: PaymentGateway)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming service locators are "bad"; they are a legitimate trade-off for tiny apps or framework-instantiated classes.
  • Calling Dagger a service locator because of component getFoo() exposure; the entry point methods are only used at the edges.
  • Letting a locator leak into domain classes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is a locator-style call unavoidable even with Dagger? → Entry points for classes you do not construct (Hilt EntryPointAccessors, ContentProviders).
  2. How do you test a class using a locator? → Reset or override the global registry per test; this is the fragile part.
  3. Does Koin make your code a locator? → Only if classes call get()/inject() themselves; constructor-injected with definitions in modules is DI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Dagger is compile-time, Koin is runtime". Senior: distinguishes pattern of use from tool, names failure timing, test isolation and scope management as the real differences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Koin app shipped a crash on a rarely visited screen because a definition was missing; no test had resolved that graph. A checkModules style test would have caught it.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through what @Inject, @Module, @Component and @Provides each do, and what Dagger actually generates.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Verifies that Dagger is not "magic" to you: it generates plain Java factories and a component implementation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @Inject on a constructor tells Dagger how to build a class. @Module with @Provides tells it how to build things it cannot construct itself (interfaces, third-party types). @Component is the interface that declares what the graph exposes; Dagger generates DaggerAppComponent implementing it, with factory classes for each binding. All of it is resolved at compile time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The annotation processor (kapt, or KSP from Dagger 2.60+; per the official KSP guide, verify exact KSP plugin version) builds a binding graph: nodes are keys (type plus optional qualifier), edges are dependencies. For every @Inject constructor it generates Foo_Factory; for each @Provides it generates Module_ProvideXFactory; for the component it generates DaggerXComponent with fields and provider objects. Missing binding, cycle or duplicate is a compile error, not a runtime crash.

@Component interface AppComponent { fun repo(): UserRepo }
           |  generated
DaggerAppComponent: private val api = ApiModule_ProvideApiFactory.provideApi()
                    fun repo() = UserRepo(api)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module
object NetworkModule {
    @Provides fun okHttp(): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder().build()
}

class UserRepo @Inject constructor(private val client: OkHttpClient)

@Component(modules = [NetworkModule::class])
interface AppComponent {
    fun userRepo(): UserRepo
}
// val c = DaggerAppComponent.create()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the component must expose or inject an entry point; unused bindings are never validated unless fullBindingGraphValidation is on.
  • Using @Module class with @Provides instead of object: generates an instance needlessly.
  • Expecting reflection; there is none.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where can you read the generated code? → build/generated/ksp or kapt output directories; it reads like handwritten wiring.
  2. Why can an unused @Provides have a bug that never surfaces? → Dagger only validates reachable bindings by default.
  3. What is fullBindingGraphValidation? → Compiler option validating all bindings in each module, default off; useful in CI for library modules.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists annotations. Senior: describes generated factories, key/graph model, compile-time validation scope, and reads generated code when debugging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Team debugged a "wrong instance" bug in minutes by opening DaggerAppComponent and seeing the provider chain, no guessing.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use @Binds and when @Provides? Is @Binds really better?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common Dagger staple; a good answer shows knowledge of generated code, not just "Binds is faster".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @Binds maps an implementation type to an interface when the implementation already has an @Inject constructor; it is an abstract method that generates no factory and no instance code. @Provides runs a body, so use it for third-party types, builders, or anything needing logic. Prefer @Binds whenever it applies.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: @Binds is an alias declaration in the graph: key UserRepository resolves to key UserRepositoryImpl. Dagger does not generate a @Provides factory class for it, so there is less generated code and less method count. @Provides generates a factory class per method and calls your function. @Binds rules: abstract, one parameter assignable to the return type, in an abstract class or interface. Mixing both in one module: use an abstract class with a companion object containing the @Provides methods (Dagger supports static provides in a companion).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module
abstract class DataModule {
    @Binds abstract fun repo(impl: UserRepositoryImpl): UserRepository

    companion object {
        @Provides fun retrofit(client: OkHttpClient): Retrofit =
            Retrofit.Builder().client(client).baseUrl("https://api.example.com/").build()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Binds with an implementation lacking @Inject constructor: missing binding error for the impl.
  • @Provides fun repo(impl: RepoImpl): Repo = impl: works but wastes a generated factory.
  • Putting @Provides in an interface module without companion/object: not allowed without static provision.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does @Binds preserve scope? → The scope annotation on the @Binds method applies to the bound key; scope can also sit on the impl class.
  2. How would you bind a different implementation per build type? → Different modules per source set or a @Provides choosing from flags.
  3. Can @Binds take a qualified parameter? → Yes, qualifiers on parameter and method let you alias qualified keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Binds is more efficient." Senior: explains no factory is generated, the abstract-plus-companion pattern, scope placement, and that the win is generated code size and clarity, not runtime speed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Converting 400 trivial @Provides aliases to @Binds reduced generated sources and shaved seconds off annotation processing in a large module.

questions.promptHtml: What does @Singleton (or any scope annotation) actually guarantee in Dagger? What is the lifetime of a scoped object?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates think @Singleton means JVM-wide singleton. It means one instance per component instance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A scope means "one instance per instance of the component that carries that scope". @Singleton is just a scope annotation, nothing special beyond naming. If you create two AppComponents you get two "singletons". The scoped object lives exactly as long as the component, so scope lifetime equals component lifetime, which you control.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A scoped binding is wrapped in DoubleCheck (thread-safe lazy memoization) in the generated component. Rules: a component can only hold bindings with its own scope annotation (or unscoped); a subcomponent may use parent scopes. Mismatch yields "@Singleton bindings may not be used in @ActivityScope component" style error. Unscoped bindings create a new instance each injection. @Reusable is a weaker cache: instance may be reused but not guaranteed, no component-lifetime obligation.

AppComponent  @Singleton  -- lives with Application
  |__ UserComponent @UserScope -- created at login, dropped at logout
        |__ ActivityComponent @ActivityScope

Anything you scope must be safe to hold for that long: scope to the shortest lifetime that is correct.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
class Cache @Inject constructor()

@Singleton
@Component(modules = [AppModule::class])
interface AppComponent { fun cache(): Cache }

val a = DaggerAppComponent.create().cache()
val b = DaggerAppComponent.create().cache() // different instance: different component

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Scoping everything @Singleton "for performance"; it extends lifetime and risks memory leaks plus thread-safety exposure.
  • Scoping mutable state without thread safety.
  • Believing scope gives lazy init: it does, but only on first request.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cost of scoped vs unscoped? → Scoped adds DoubleCheck indirection and holds memory; unscoped allocates per injection. Most objects are cheap and should be unscoped.
  2. @Reusable use case? → Immutable, cheap but not free objects (formatters), where you accept occasional duplicates.
  3. How do you drop a scoped object? → Drop the component reference; there is no per-binding eviction.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Singleton is one instance". Senior: instance per component, DoubleCheck, scope matching rules, and "scope only what must share state".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics batcher scoped @Singleton accumulated a reference to a user session; after logout it retained PII until process death.

questions.promptHtml: How do qualifiers work, and why prefer custom qualifier annotations to @Named?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Type-keyed graph means two bindings of the same type need disambiguation; checks understanding of keys.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dagger's key is the type plus an optional qualifier. When you need two OkHttpClients or two CoroutineDispatchers, you mark both the provider and the injection site with the same qualifier. @Named("io") is a string and typo-prone; a custom @Qualifier annotation is checked by the compiler and refactor-safe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without a qualifier two @Provides returning CoroutineDispatcher collide: "CoroutineDispatcher is bound multiple times". Qualifier annotations are compared by annotation type and members. In Kotlin, remember use-site targets for constructor properties: for @Inject constructor(@IoDispatcher private val d: CoroutineDispatcher) it works on the parameter; for field injection use @field:IoDispatcher or @set:.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class IoDispatcher
@Qualifier @Retention(AnnotationRetention.BINARY) annotation class DefaultDispatcher

@Module
object DispatcherModule {
    @Provides @IoDispatcher fun io(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
    @Provides @DefaultDispatcher fun def(): CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default
}

class Repo @Inject constructor(@IoDispatcher private val io: CoroutineDispatcher)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @Named("io") on provider but @Named("IO") on consumer: compile-time missing binding, but confusing.
  • Field injection with Kotlin lateinit and no @field: target: qualifier silently attaches to the wrong element, causing missing binding.
  • Qualifying everything; qualify only when types collide.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a qualifier carry parameters? → Yes, annotation members (for example @Api(Version.V2)), compared by value.
  2. Why inject dispatchers at all? → Testability: replace with StandardTestDispatcher in tests.
  3. Qualifier on @Binds? → Supported; qualifies the produced key.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: uses @Named. Senior: custom qualifiers, Kotlin use-site targets, and ties to dispatcher injection for tests.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A typo'd @Named("authClient") across two modules was found only in CI; custom qualifiers removed that class of bug.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between injecting T, Lazy<T> and Provider<T>? When would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests startup cost thinking and understanding of scope and instance creation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: T is created when the owner is created. Lazy<T> defers creation to first get() and then caches that instance for that injection site. Provider<T> calls the binding every get(): new instance for unscoped bindings, the single instance for scoped ones. Use Lazy to defer costly work off the startup path; use Provider when you need fresh instances on demand.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lazy<T> memoizes per injection site, not globally: two classes each injecting Lazy<Foo> of an unscoped Foo get two different instances. For a scoped binding, both ultimately resolve to the scoped instance. Provider<T> is the thing Dagger already uses internally; it also breaks construction cycles (A(B), B(Provider<A>)) though cycles are usually a design smell. Beware Provider<T> of a type needing a different scope than where it is injected.

T            : constructed during owner construction
Lazy<T>      : constructed on first .get(); same instance afterwards (this site)
Provider<T>  : constructed on every .get() if unscoped; scoped => same instance

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class HomeViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val heavyReporter: Lazy<CrashReporter>,    // dagger.Lazy
    private val rowProvider: Provider<RowFormatter>    // fresh formatter per call
) {
    fun onError(t: Throwable) = heavyReporter.get().report(t)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Importing kotlin.Lazy instead of dagger.Lazy; Dagger will not treat it as a request for lazy.
  • Using Lazy to hide a circular dependency forever.
  • Assuming Lazy makes the dependency's own dependencies lazy; only that binding is deferred.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Lazy<T> avoid class loading? → Not necessarily; the generated factory exists and may load; it defers instance creation.
  2. How would you reduce cold-start DI cost? → Lazy on heavy singletons, move work off main, trace with Perfetto.
  3. Thread safety? → Lazy is thread-safe via double-checked locking in generated code.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Lazy is delayed creation." Senior: per-site memoization, Provider semantics with scopes, cycle-breaking caveats, and the cold-start measurement angle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching four heavy SDK wrappers to Lazy cut 90 ms from the application-create trace on low-end devices.

questions.promptHtml: Subcomponents versus component dependencies: how do they differ, and which would you pick?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most-asked Dagger design question; reveals graph design thinking and awareness of Hilt's choice.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A subcomponent is a child graph: it sees every binding of its parent, has one parent, and is created from the parent. Component dependencies are two independent components where the dependent only sees what the dependency component explicitly exposes as provision methods. I default to subcomponents for lifecycle hierarchies (app, user, activity) and use dependencies when I want a hard API boundary between separately compiled modules. Hilt uses the subcomponent model.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Subcomponent:   Parent graph  ==inherits==> Child graph (sees all bindings)
Dependencies:   A exposes fun foo(): Foo  --> B(dependencies = [A]) sees only Foo

Subcomponents are generated as part of the root component's code, so the whole tree compiles together, and scoping is enforced hierarchically. Component dependencies each compile alone, which suits independent feature modules because the contract is the exposed interface, but every needed binding must be hand-exposed, and scopes must differ (a dependent component cannot share the same scope annotation as its dependency).

Trade-offs: subcomponents are less boilerplate and clearer lifetimes but tie children to the parent's whole graph; dependencies give encapsulation at the price of exposure plumbing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Subcomponent(modules = [UserModule::class])
@UserScope
interface UserComponent {
    @Subcomponent.Factory interface Factory { fun create(@BindsInstance user: User): UserComponent }
}

@Module(subcomponents = [UserComponent::class])
object AppBindings

@Singleton @Component(modules = [AppBindings::class])
interface AppComponent { fun userComponentFactory(): UserComponent.Factory }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using dependent components and forgetting to expose bindings: "cannot be provided" error pointing at a parent that has it internally.
  • Same scope on dependent and dependency: error.
  • Letting the child outlive its parent reference conceptually; it still holds the parent graph.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a subcomponent have two parents? → No, one parent.
  2. Which gives better incremental build? → Dependencies compile independently; a subcomponent changes can force regeneration of the root component. Measure in your project.
  3. Why does Hilt pick subcomponents? → Fixed lifecycle tree mapped to Android classes, less user wiring.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "subcomponent sees all parent bindings". Senior: adds scope rules, the encapsulation vs boilerplate trade-off, build implications, and the user-session pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature team used dependent components for isolation and then spent weeks exposing 40 provision methods; moving to subcomponents under the app component removed that plumbing.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate adds a cache and the build fails. Code:

@Singleton
class ProfileCache @Inject constructor(private val api: ProfileApi)

@ActivityScope
@Component(dependencies = [AppComponent::class])
interface ProfileComponent { fun inject(a: ProfileActivity) }

@Singleton
@Component(modules = [NetModule::class])
interface AppComponent

Error: ProfileComponent (unscoped) ... @Singleton ProfileCache may not be reference from a component with scope @ActivityScope. They then "fix" it by marking ProfileCache as @ActivityScope, and QA reports that profile data is stale after navigating away and back, plus cache hits are 0%.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, why did the "fix" cause new symptoms, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just change the annotations until it compiles." Misses that scope mismatch is a lifetime declaration, not a lint, and that the fix changed behavior.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the cache meant to survive Activity recreation? Is it per user? Who else reads it? Is ProfileComponent created per Activity instance?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the scope change on ProfileCache so data semantics are unchanged; unblock the build by not injecting the cache directly into the activity component.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) scope mismatch: a @Singleton class cannot be provided by an @ActivityScope component that only depends on AppComponent; (b) the fix made the cache per activity component instance, so each new Activity makes a new cache (0% hit rate); (c) the cache needs to be exposed from AppComponent, which owns it.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the full Dagger error (it names the offending scope); inspect generated DaggerProfileComponent to see DoubleCheck wrapping; log ProfileCache identity hash across two Activity instances.
  5. Root cause: @Singleton bindings belong to the component annotated @Singleton. A component depending on AppComponent can only get what AppComponent exposes. Scoping the cache @ActivityScope gave one instance per ProfileComponent, which is recreated per Activity.
  6. Fix: Short-term: expose fun profileCache(): ProfileCache on AppComponent and keep @Singleton. Long-term: if the cache should reset on logout, move it to a user-scoped subcomponent.
@Singleton @Component(modules = [NetModule::class])
interface AppComponent { fun profileCache(): ProfileCache }
  1. Prevention: Code review rule: never change a scope to make the compiler pass without stating the intended lifetime; add a unit test asserting same instance across two Activity components.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not @Reusable (no guarantee of single cache); not a Kotlin object global, losing testability.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the cache must reset on logout? → Put it in a @UserScope subcomponent and drop that component at logout.
  • What if the app uses Hilt? → @Singleton maps to SingletonComponent; Activities get ActivityComponent as a descendant and see it automatically.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "make it compile" scope change turned a shared image cache into a per-screen cache, memory use doubled and hit rate fell to zero, noticed only in a perf dashboard two releases later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes annotations until it compiles.
  • Hire: identifies scope mismatch and exposes the binding from the owning component.
  • Strong hire: also reasons about lifetime ownership, logout reset, verification by instance identity, and prevention.

questions.promptHtml: What are Dagger multibindings and where have you used @IntoSet / @IntoMap?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A plugin-architecture signal; tests knowledge of how to avoid a central switch statement.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Multibindings let separate modules contribute entries to one Set<T> or Map<K,V> that Dagger assembles. It is how I build plugin lists: interceptors, initializers, analytics trackers, ViewModel factories keyed by class. The consumer injects Set<Initializer> and never knows who contributed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: @IntoSet adds one element; @ElementsIntoSet adds a collection (and can supply an empty set); @IntoMap plus a @MapKey adds a keyed entry. Per the Dagger docs, duplicate set elements are silently collapsed (Set semantics), but duplicate map keys are a compile error. @Multibinds declares a set/map that may be empty so injection compiles with zero contributions. Map<K, Provider<V>> defers instance creation, which is how ViewModel-factory maps work. Order of set elements is not guaranteed; do not depend on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Module
interface InitModule {
    @Binds @IntoSet fun crash(i: CrashInitializer): AppInitializer
    @Binds @IntoSet fun ads(i: AdsInitializer): AppInitializer
    @Multibinds fun defaults(): Set<AppInitializer> // allow empty
}

class AppStartup @Inject constructor(private val inits: Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards AppInitializer>) {
    fun run() = inits.forEach { it.init() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Missing @JvmSuppressWildcards in Kotlin: Dagger sees Set<? extends X> and reports missing binding.
  • Depending on set order for init ordering.
  • Using a Map<Class<*>, Provider<..>> for everything; it becomes a hidden service locator.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Map key by enum or class? → @ClassKey, @StringKey, or custom @MapKey.
  2. Cross-component duplicates? → Map duplicate-key detection across component boundaries needs mapMultibindingDuplicateDetectionFix option (default disabled per Dagger docs).
  3. How to enforce initializer order? → Add explicit priority or dependency in the interface and sort; do not rely on set order.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "put several implementations in a set". Senior: map vs set semantics, @Multibinds empty case, Kotlin wildcard trap, Provider maps, and the locator trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Startup initializers moved from a 300-line Application.onCreate into set multibinding, letting each feature own its initialization and making ordering bugs explicit.

questions.promptHtml: What does Dagger validate at compile time, and how do you read a long Dagger error to find the real cause?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everyone hits the 80-line error; seniors know how to read it quickly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dagger validates the full reachable graph: missing bindings, duplicate bindings, scope mismatches, cycles and nullability. The error prints a dependency trace from the entry point down to the missing key. I read it bottom-up: the last line is the unsatisfied key, the lines above are the chain that required it, and the top is the component entry point.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Typical shape:

error: [Dagger/MissingBinding] com.app.PaymentApi cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method.
    com.app.PaymentApi is injected at
        com.app.CheckoutRepo(api)
    com.app.CheckoutRepo is injected at
        com.app.CheckoutViewModel(repo)
    com.app.CheckoutViewModel is injected at
        com.app.MainActivity.viewModel
    com.app.MainActivity is injected at
        com.app.AppComponent.inject(activity)

Triage: (1) missing: check the module is listed on the right component or @InstallIn; (2) duplicate: two modules bind the same key, error lists both locations; (3) scope: component scope vs binding scope; (4) qualifier/wildcard mismatch (Kotlin Set<@JvmSuppressWildcards X>); (5) interface bound with no @Binds. With subcomponents, Dagger may report "missing in the subcomponent graph" including a "this requires ... may be provided in <other component>" hint.

Dagger only validates what an entry point can reach, so unreachable broken bindings pass until used; fullBindingGraphValidation (default off) validates everything in modules.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Duplicate binding fix: keep one, or qualify
@Module object A { @Provides fun client(): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient() }
@Module object B { @Provides fun client(): OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient() } // [Dagger/DuplicateBindings]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Fixing the top of the trace instead of the bottom key.
  • Missing generated-code errors that are actually kapt/KSP stub failures: the first error in the build is the cause; later errors cascade.
  • Ignoring "incremental processing" stale output: clean the module when generated errors look impossible.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Error mentions a @Nullable mismatch? → Provider returns nullable and consumer is non-null; mark both or change provider.
  2. Dagger error vs Kotlin errors showing together? → Resolve Kotlin compile errors first; Dagger runs on stubs and misleads.
  3. How do you catch broken bindings in library modules? → Enable full binding graph validation in CI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Dagger says something is missing, so I add it." Senior: reads the trace bottom-up, classifies the error family, knows the cascade and stale-output traps.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 300-line Dagger error was solved in two minutes by seeing the real cause: a module not added to the component after a package move.

questions.promptHtml: How does Dagger implement a scoped binding at runtime, and what does its generated component look like?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use Dagger from people who can reason about its performance and thread safety.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dagger generates a class implementing my component. For each binding it generates a factory; for scoped ones it holds a Provider<T> field in the component wrapped in DoubleCheck, which memoizes the first created instance with double-checked locking. Unscoped bindings are inlined: just new Foo(dep1, dep2) at the call site. No reflection.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Default mode builds Provider fields eagerly in the component constructor; each Provider is a Factory instance. With fastInit mode (-Adagger.fastInit=enabled, default off in plain Dagger; Hilt enables it) the component generates fewer classes: a single switching provider class with an integer id, trading some runtime branching for fewer class loads and a faster startup. Fast init mostly matters for startup of huge graphs.

Thread safety: DoubleCheck.get() uses a volatile field with synchronized creation, so scoped objects are safely published but their own internal state is not synchronized.

@Singleton Foo   -->  private Provider<Foo> fooProvider = DoubleCheck.provider(Foo_Factory.create(...));
unscoped Bar     -->  new Bar(foo())   (inline in the consumer's factory)

Cycle break: Dagger inserts a DelegateFactory for a Provider cycle and sets it after creation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Gradle option to try fast init (verify effect with a benchmark)
// build.gradle.kts
ksp { arg("dagger.fastInit", "enabled") }   // kapt: javacOptions / arguments { arg(...) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming scoped = synchronized object: only creation is synchronized.
  • Enabling fastInit blindly without measuring both startup and APK size.
  • Reading generated code once and assuming it never changes between Dagger versions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Hilt turn on fastInit by default? → Per the Dagger option docs Hilt enables it; the goal is cold-start friendliness on mobile.
  2. What happens with a binding used by both a scoped and unscoped consumer? → The scoped one returns the shared instance, the unscoped one gets a new instance of the unscoped binding only.
  3. Memory cost of scoped bindings? → One field per scoped binding in the component, alive as long as the component.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Dagger generates factories." Senior: names DoubleCheck, Provider fields, fast-init trade-off, delegate cycle breaking, and thread-safety limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Class-loading time of a thousand generated factories showed up in cold-start traces; fast-init mode plus lazy providers brought application creation down measurably (measure, do not assume).

questions.contextHtml:
You are on call-adjacent: the nightly build of a 40-module app turns red after a merge. Error from :app:kaptReleaseKotlin:

[Dagger/MissingBinding] com.shop.cart.CartApi cannot be provided without an @Inject constructor or an @Provides-annotated method.
  com.shop.cart.CartApi is injected at com.shop.cart.CartRepositoryImpl(api)
  ...
  com.shop.app.AppComponent.checkoutComponent()
[Dagger/DuplicateBindings] com.shop.core.Analytics is bound multiple times:
  @Binds Analytics FirebaseAnalytics in AnalyticsModule
  @Provides Analytics in LegacyAnalyticsModule

Two teams merged in the same hour. Debug build passes; release fails. Build is 14 minutes, so each try is expensive. Also a red herring: a Kotlin warning about deprecated kapt.use.worker.api.
questions.promptHtml: How do you triage and fix this quickly, and prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Re-run the build, clean caches, or add random @Provides to silence errors. Does not separate the two errors or notice why release differs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What merged? Do debug and release use different module sets (source sets, flavors)? Is LegacyAnalyticsModule meant to be deleted? Which team owns CartApi?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the last merge if the main branch must be green; otherwise fix forward in a small PR within the hour. Tell both teams.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) CartApi binding lives in a module that exists only in debug source set or in a module not added to the component; (b) the duplicate is a leftover from half-finished migration; (c) release-only R8/flavor config swaps modules; (d) the kapt worker warning is unrelated.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read each error separately; grep @Provides.*CartApi/@Binds.*CartApi; check @Module(includes=...) and component modules= lists; compare src/debug vs src/main; run ./gradlew :app:kaptReleaseKotlin only (not full build) to iterate in minutes; for cross-module wiring use --scan to confirm which modules are on the release classpath.
  5. Root cause (typical): A new binding for CartApi was added in src/debug module copy, so release lacks it; and the analytics migration added the new @Binds without removing the legacy @Provides. Dagger reports both because it validates the whole reachable graph.
  6. Fix: Short-term: move the CartApi binding to src/main, delete the legacy provider. Long-term: add one module per feature and make the release/debug variance explicit via a dedicated DebugOverridesModule only for debug-only things.
  7. Prevention: CI job that compiles both variants on PR; fullBindingGraphValidation=ERROR for library modules; CODEOWNERS on DI modules; a merge queue to serialize rapid merges.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not suppress with @Provides fakes in release; not silence validation; not hide it with @Named hacks to make duplicates unique.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Only one error appears locally but CI shows both? → Incremental processing hid it; run clean kapt locally or --rerun-tasks for that task.
  • The error trace is missing entry point info? → Build with --stacktrace and open the first error in the log, not the summary.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two migrations landed within an hour and each passed its own PR; only the merged tree had a duplicate key. A PR-level "merge-result build" check removed that class of failure.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cleans and retries; random fixes.
  • Hire: separates the two errors, finds variant difference, fixes bindings.
  • Strong hire: iterates with the single kapt task, adds CI variant compile and ownership prevention, explains why unreachable bindings stay silent.

questions.promptHtml: How does Dagger's assisted injection work, and why is it needed for objects with runtime parameters?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mixing runtime values (an ID) with graph dependencies is a daily problem; the old answer is hand-written factories.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Some constructor parameters come from the graph (repository) and some from the caller at runtime (itemId). @AssistedInject on the constructor marks runtime params with @Assisted; an @AssistedFactory interface declares a create(...) taking only the assisted params. Dagger generates the factory, supplying graph params itself.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Without it you write a factory class by hand that holds the graph dependencies and takes the runtime ones: boilerplate that must be updated whenever the constructor changes. @AssistedFactory generates it. Assisted params with the same type need a distinguishing string in @Assisted("name"). The factory itself is injectable and unscoped by default. Dagger validates that the factory method's parameters match assisted params exactly (types and order-insensitive via identifiers). Per the compiler options docs, strictAssistedInjectValidation defaults to enabled and requires library @AssistedInject types to have been processed by Dagger.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class PlayerPresenter @AssistedInject constructor(
    private val repo: TrackRepository,
    @Assisted private val trackId: String,
    @Assisted("start") private val startMs: Long
) {
    @AssistedFactory
    interface Factory { fun create(trackId: String, @Assisted("start") startMs: Long): PlayerPresenter }
}

class PlayerFragment @Inject constructor(private val factory: PlayerPresenter.Factory) {
    fun make() = factory.create("t1", 0L)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the identifier when two assisted params share a type: duplicate key error.
  • Scoping an assisted-injected type: unsupported.
  • Using it for something with only graph dependencies: plain @Inject is right.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Hilt build on it? → @HiltViewModel(assistedFactory = ...) for ViewModels with runtime args (see the Hilt chunk).
  2. Alternative without it? → Pass the runtime value through a method, not the constructor.
  3. Can the factory expose multiple create methods? → No, one abstract method per @AssistedFactory.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it creates a factory." Senior: explains the boilerplate problem, matching identifiers, scoping limits, and prefers method params when the object lives longer than the call.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-written factory silently dropped a new dependency in default arguments; assisted injection made the compiler enforce the wiring.

questions.promptHtml: What does Dagger cost at build time, and how do KSP and kapt change that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: DI choices show up in build time; seniors can name mitigations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: kapt generates Java stubs of Kotlin sources then runs javac annotation processing, which is slow and often forces full re-processing. KSP processes Kotlin symbols directly and is generally faster. Dagger's KSP support is described as stable from Dagger 2.60 with a matching KSP version (verify the exact numbers in current docs). Beyond tooling, graph size and component placement control how much regenerates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Costs: (1) stub generation for kapt; (2) validation and generation of the component and factories, which scale with graph size; (3) the root component is a single large generated file; changing any binding it depends on regenerates it and recompiles the Java output. Mitigations: move to KSP (and migrate all other processors too: per Dagger KSP guide KSP cannot resolve types generated by kapt/javac processors, so mixing is limited); keep modules small and focused so incremental processing has less to redo; avoid formatGeneratedSource (slows builds); use implementation not api for DI modules to limit recompile propagation; consider whether subcomponents vs dependent components fit module boundaries. Verify with Gradle build scans and --profile, looking at kaptGenerateStubs and kapt task time per module (build performance chunk covers general Gradle tuning).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts (module)
plugins { id("com.google.devtools.ksp") }
dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.dagger:dagger:<version>")
    ksp("com.google.dagger:dagger-compiler:<version>") // 2.60+ for KSP, per docs; verify
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Moving Dagger to KSP while a dependent processor (AutoFactory, older Hilt compiler) stays on kapt: unresolved generated types.
  • Putting every @Provides in one gigantic module in :app.
  • Measuring only clean builds; incremental behavior matters more daily.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure? → Build scan task timeline; compare kapt vs ksp task durations per module.
  2. Does modularization help or hurt? → Helps incremental builds if graphs split; hurts with many small modules each running processors.
  3. Any experimental flag? → The KSP guide mentions ksp.experimental.psi.resolution=true as experimental, verify before use.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "KSP is faster." Senior: why (no stubs), caveats on mixed processors, root component regeneration, and measures with build scans before and after.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving a large app from kapt to KSP in stages took annotation processing off the critical path for incremental builds; the blocker was one legacy processor.

questions.contextHtml: A 60-module app, 90 engineers. Incremental build after touching a single @Provides in :core:network takes 6 min 40 s; a clean build is 17 min. Build scan: kaptGenerateStubsDebugKotlin + kaptDebugKotlin total 3.4 min on :app alone and 20-40 s on 30 feature modules. All Dagger modules are in feature modules and all components in :app. Developers are asking to "remove Dagger". The app targets 8M MAU, release cadence weekly.
questions.promptHtml: How do you reduce the DI-related build cost, and would you remove Dagger?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to Koin, it has no codegen." Ignores the runtime-safety and startup trade-offs and doesn't measure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 6:40 on CI or laptops? Are build cache and configuration cache on? Which processors run besides Dagger (Room, Moshi, Glide)? Is :app a god module?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable Gradle build cache and parallel; ensure org.gradle.caching=true on CI with remote cache. Nothing else risky.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) kapt stub generation dominates because everything is on kapt; (b) api dependencies mean a core change invalidates 30 modules; (c) :app component is huge and always regenerates; (d) other processors are the real hog.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build scan timeline and per-task attribution; --profile; test: touch a leaf @Provides vs touch a core type; list which processors run per module with ./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration kapt.
  5. Root cause: kapt in :app re-runs on any change affecting stubs, plus an oversized root component that recompiles in Java.
  6. Fix: Short-term: migrate Dagger and compatible processors to KSP module by module (Dagger KSP stable from 2.60 per docs; verify), turn on KSP incremental. Mid-term: shrink :app: move feature subcomponents' binding modules toward feature-owned code with a stable entry point interface; use implementation. Long-term: evaluate whether graph size justifies Dagger; compare against Hilt's aggregation cost before concluding.
  7. Prevention: Track kapt/ksp task time in CI dashboards; budget alert at +10%; convention plugin forbidding kapt where KSP exists.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite DI to a runtime container to save 3 minutes: lose compile-time safety on a 8M MAU app; not merge modules to cut processor invocations before measuring.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• KSP migration breaks on one processor? → Keep that module on kapt, isolate it so it doesn't force stubs for others.
  • Leadership wants a number? → Run the same three change types (leaf, core, signature) on kapt vs ksp and report medians, not one run.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team blamed Dagger for slow builds; the scan showed Room and a custom processor on kapt in the same modules, and the Dagger share was under a third of the time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swap DI library.
  • Hire: measures with scans, moves to KSP, reduces regeneration.
  • Strong hire: separates processors, change-type benchmarking, trade-off of runtime DI, and CI budgets.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review on a PR in a 2M DAU app. Crash reports after launch show kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property analytics has not been initialized on 0.4% of sessions (all after process death restore), and a LeakCanary report shows ImageLoader retaining a destroyed CheckoutActivity.

@Singleton
class ImageLoader @Inject constructor(private val context: Context) // bound to Activity via @Provides in ActivityModule

object Injector { lateinit var component: AppComponent }  // set in MainActivity.onCreate

class CartFragment : Fragment() {
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics
    override fun onAttach(c: Context) { super.onAttach(c); Injector.component.inject(this) }
}

class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(private val component: AppComponent) : ViewModel() {
    fun price() = component.pricing().compute()
}
questions.promptHtml: Identify every anti-pattern, rank by risk, and propose fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notes only the leak. Misses the global-holder initialization-order bug (process death restores a Fragment before MainActivity.onCreate) and the component-as-dependency service-locator smell.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Context in ImageLoader the app or activity context? Does Injector.component get set in Application? What restores CartFragment?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set Injector.component in Application.onCreate (not an Activity), and bind Context to application context in the @Singleton path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Injector is set from an Activity: after process death the system recreates the Fragment (or a different entry like a notification target) before MainActivity.onCreate runs; (b) @Singleton holding an Activity context leaks; (c) injecting AppComponent into a ViewModel is a service locator and prevents testing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce via "Don't keep activities" plus adb shell am kill restore; LeakCanary trace shows ImageLoader.context -> CheckoutActivity; unit test that constructs CheckoutViewModel with a fake: impossible without the component.
  5. Root cause: Initialization order tied to an Activity; scope longer than the injected object's lifetime; component injected as a locator.
  6. Fix:
class App : Application() { lateinit var component: AppComponent; override fun onCreate() { super.onCreate(); component = DaggerAppComponent.factory().create(this) } }
@Module object AppCtx { @Provides @Singleton fun ctx(app: App): Context = app } // not an Activity
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(private val pricing: PricingEngine) : ViewModel()
  1. Prevention: Lint/Konsist rule: no classes depending on *Component; leak tests in CI for scoped types; reviewing checklist "what is the longest lifetime that touches this object".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not move to a static global with null checks; not mark analytics nullable to avoid the crash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need the activity for a UI-bound helper? → Scope it to an activity component, never @Singleton.
  • Why not just keep Injector? → Entry via Application is fine; it is the initialization site and the locator use in classes that is wrong.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A crash cluster appeared only after OS kill; the injection happened in the wrong lifecycle callback and nobody could reproduce it without forced process death.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds only the leak.
  • Hire: finds leak, init order, and component injection.
  • Strong hire: ranks by risk, reproduces via process death, fixes with lifetime reasoning and lint prevention.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech app (1.5M DAU) supports account switching. Support reports that after switching from account A to B, about 1 in 800 sessions briefly shows A's balance. Heap dumps show AccountRepository (annotated @Singleton) holds userId and an in-memory StateFlow<Balance>. The logout code does accountRepo.clear(), but an in-flight refresh() coroutine launched in a @Singleton scope writes A's response after clear(). Metrics: p95 refresh 1.8 s, switch takes under 300 ms. Red herring: the cache TTL was recently changed from 60 s to 30 s.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, fix, and how DI structure should change.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Clear the cache properly and add a null check." Treats symptom, keeps user data in an app-lifetime scope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is user data in any other singleton? Is the response tagged by user? How is the coroutine scope created and cancelled? Is there PII exposure (compliance impact)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tag responses with userId and drop writes where it no longer matches; ship as a hotfix behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) race between clear() and in-flight refresh (matches 1.8 s vs 300 ms); (b) per-user state in an app-scoped object; (c) TTL change (red herring: it changes frequency, not correctness).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a fake API delaying 2 s and a test that switches accounts mid-flight; log object identity; heap dump to see which singletons reference user data.
  5. Root cause: User-lifetime state lives in @Singleton, so its lifetime is wrong; manual clear() cannot cancel work it does not own.
  6. Fix: Introduce a user-scoped subcomponent created at login and discarded at logout; its coroutine scope is cancelled on teardown.
@UserScope class AccountRepository @Inject constructor(@UserScopeCoroutines private val scope: CoroutineScope)
class SessionManager @Inject constructor(private val f: UserComponent.Factory) {
    var current: UserComponent? = null
    fun login(u: User) { current?.close(); current = f.create(u) }
    fun logout() { current?.close(); current = null }
}

where close() cancels the scope. Long-term: all per-user bindings live in this component. 7. Prevention: Architecture test that @Singleton classes do not hold user identifiers; a test for account-switch races; blameless review notes the scope audit. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not more if (userId == ...) checks scattered; not kill the process on logout as a shortcut (hurts UX); accept extra component plumbing as the cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Background WorkManager job runs after logout? → Workers must fetch the current session or be cancelled by session id; do not capture the old component.
  • Entities cached on disk? → Key by user id or wipe on logout; separate concern from DI scope.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The fix was less about the race than discovering seven singletons holding per-user data, each guarded by a hand-written clear() that someone forgot to update.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: patches the cache.
  • Hire: identifies race and scope mismatch.
  • Strong hire: user-scoped subcomponent with cancellable scope, compliance awareness, and architecture tests.

questions.promptHtml: How do you pass runtime objects into a Dagger component, and what are @BindsInstance, @Component.Factory and @BindsOptionalOf for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Application context, user, config: how seniors wire the roots of the graph without static state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: @BindsInstance on a @Component.Factory (or Builder) parameter makes a runtime object available as a binding without a module. Factories are preferred to builders because the compiler forces all required params. @BindsOptionalOf declares a dependency that may or may not be bound, injected as Optional<T>, so a feature works whether or not another module supplies something.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Modules with constructor parameters are the older way; @BindsInstance is simpler and avoids module instances. For components with required modules/instances, the factory's signature documents requirements. Optional bindings suit debug-only extras (a debug overlay) or flavors: declare @BindsOptionalOf in the main module, provide in the debug module. The injection site uses Optional<T> (Guava, java.util.Optional or Dagger's accepted forms: verify which Optional types your Dagger version supports for Kotlin).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
@Component(modules = [AppModule::class])
interface AppComponent {
    @Component.Factory interface Factory {
        fun create(@BindsInstance app: Application, @BindsInstance config: AppConfig): AppComponent
    }
}

@Module interface DebugHooks { @BindsOptionalOf fun overlay(): DebugOverlay }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• @BindsInstance with nullable types without @Nullable/qualifier consideration.
  • Binding Activity into the app component; lifetime mismatch.
  • Using optional bindings to dodge fixing a real missing binding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Builder vs Factory? → Factory is compile-checked for required params, less boilerplate; Builder is legacy-friendly.
  2. Runtime object per screen? → Subcomponent factory with @BindsInstance, or assisted injection for single objects.
  3. Test impact? → Create the component in tests with fake instances without a static holder.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: passes Context through a module. Senior: factory with @BindsInstance, optional bindings for variants, and no static holders.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Debug-only tools were wired with optional bindings so release code had zero references to debug classes, a requirement for the security review.

questions.contextHtml: A super-app with 14 mini-feature teams wants each team to register a screen "entry" (route to destination) without editing a central file. Currently FeatureRegistry has a 600-line when statement causing merge conflicts about 5 times a week. Teams propose: (A) Map<Class<out Feature>, Provider<Feature>> multibinding, (B) runtime reflection scanning, (C) a Kotlin object registry each module registers into at startup. Cold start budget: +20 ms max. Two teams already shipped duplicate keys by copy-paste.
questions.promptHtml: Which option and why? How do you make it safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks (C) because it is "simplest". Ignores startup ordering, duplicate keys at runtime, and testability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are features in separate Gradle modules (so the app component must see them)? Do all features need to exist at startup? Do we need dynamic feature modules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed beyond stopping the weekly conflicts; move one feature as a pilot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (A) fits best: compile-time validation, no reflection; (C) has registration order and forgotten-registration risk; (B) costs startup and R8 pain.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with two features; check cold-start trace for registry creation cost; check duplicate key behavior (compile error for maps within a component).
  5. Root cause: Central switch creates a shared edit point; multibindings invert ownership: each module contributes.
  6. Fix:
@MapKey annotation class FeatureKey(val value: String)
@Module interface CartFeatureModule { @Binds @IntoMap @FeatureKey("cart") fun cart(f: CartFeature): Feature }
class Registry @Inject constructor(private val features: Map<String, @JvmSuppressWildcards Provider<Feature>>) {
    fun open(key: String) = features.getValue(key).get()
}

Provider map keeps creation lazy, protecting the 20 ms budget. 7. Prevention: Unit test that every expected key exists; map key duplicate detection is compile-time within a component (note the cross-component option mentioned in the Dagger docs, default off); ownership docs for key naming. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The :app component must include every feature module (coupling at the composition root, acceptable); not reflection scanning; not a global mutable registry.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Dynamic feature modules not in the app classpath? → Multibinding cannot see them; use a different mechanism such as service lookup via the feature's own component/entry point.
  • Need ordering? → Put priority in the contract; do not rely on map iteration.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving to a map multibinding eliminated the merge hotspot, but a typo'd string key sent users to the wrong screen; enum or class keys were the fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: chooses global object registry.
  • Hire: picks multibinding with Providers and explains compile-time safety.
  • Strong hire: handles startup budget, dynamic modules limit, key typing and tests.

questions.contextHtml: A 6-year-old app (3M DAU, ~400 classes use object singletons and Injector.get()) will adopt Dagger. 25 engineers, weekly releases, crash-free rate target 99.8%, no feature freeze allowed. Previous attempt to convert everything in one PR was abandoned after a 3-week merge conflict marathon.
questions.promptHtml: How would you migrate, and how do you keep it safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Big bang on a branch." Or adopting Dagger without a rule for new code.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the 5 most painful singletons for tests? Who owns Application/Activity bases? Is a Hilt migration eventually planned (affects component design)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze the growth: new code uses constructor injection; no new Injector.get() calls (lint check).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risk sits in initialization order (singletons with side effects), scope changes, and threading.
  4. How I'd verify each: Startup trace comparison per step; crash-free monitoring by version; unit tests per migrated class.
  5. Root cause of past failure: Unbounded PR size, coupled with changing behavior and structure simultaneously.
  6. Fix (plan): (1) Add Dagger with an AppComponent that wraps existing singletons via @Provides returning the legacy object; (2) convert leaf classes to @Inject constructors, leave legacy callers using a bridge; (3) migrate Activities/Fragments to field injection; (4) delete bridges in the end. Each step shippable.
@Module object LegacyBridge { @Provides @Singleton fun prefs(): Prefs = LegacyPrefs } // temporary
  1. Prevention: Lint rule banning the locator in new code; metrics on count of remaining legacy calls; staged rollout.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite behavior while moving wiring; not convert modules with no test coverage first; accept a period with two styles coexisting.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Startup regression after step 1? → Introduce Lazy or defer heavy singletons; verify with Perfetto.
  • Team resists? → Show the first test that was impossible before.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The migration succeeded only after the bridge-and-count approach; a burn-down chart of legacy calls kept management patient.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big bang.
  • Hire: incremental bridge, leaf-first conversion.
  • Strong hire: guardrail lint, metrics, startup monitoring, and behavior-vs-structure separation.

questions.promptHtml: How do you model a user-session or flow-scoped lifetime with Dagger subcomponents, and what can go wrong?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests lifetime thinking beyond @Singleton: login, checkout flows, per-account graphs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I define a @Subcomponent with its own scope annotation and a @Subcomponent.Factory, held by a session manager. Creating it starts the lifetime, nulling it ends it. Everything scoped to it dies with the reference, provided nothing longer-lived holds on to those instances.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules: the subcomponent's scope differs from the parent's; the parent declares the subcomponent via @Module(subcomponents = ...) or by exposing the factory. Children see parent bindings but not the reverse. Pitfalls: (1) a parent-scoped object capturing a child object (leak, and logically a dependency inversion); (2) coroutines or callbacks launched in the child that outlive teardown unless their scope is cancelled; (3) restoring after process death: the component must be rebuilt from persisted state (user id) at app start, before screens inject; (4) thread-safety of the holder reference.

AppComponent(@Singleton)
   |-- SessionManager holds UserComponent?  (null when logged out)
          |-- UserComponent(@UserScope): repos, DB handle, coroutine scope

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Scope annotation class UserScope
@UserScope @Subcomponent
interface UserComponent {
    fun repo(): AccountRepository
    @Subcomponent.Factory interface Factory { fun create(@BindsInstance user: User): UserComponent }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Injecting UserComponent anywhere that can run when logged out: NPE.
  • Forgetting to cancel child coroutine scopes.
  • Rebuilding the component on every configuration change.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Hilt do this? → No custom components in Hilt; use a manually managed scope or entry points (see the Hilt chunk).
  2. How to test? → Build the subcomponent with fakes using a test parent component.
  3. Memory proof? → Heap dump after logout to see zero instances of @UserScope classes.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "make a subcomponent". Senior: teardown semantics, process-death rebuild, coroutine cancellation, and leak verification.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Account-switch bugs in finance apps are usually lifetime bugs, not logic bugs.

questions.contextHtml: After upgrading to a new release with 140 more @Inject classes, cold start p50 on low-end devices (2 GB RAM, Android 10) went from 1.9 s to 2.4 s; ANR rate rose from 0.3% to 0.5% on startup. A Perfetto trace shows DaggerAppComponent.<init> taking 310 ms on the main thread and a Class.forName-like burst of loading *_Factory classes. The team suspects "Dagger is slow". Red herring: a new analytics SDK also initializes at Application.onCreate (40 ms).
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix the startup regression.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move Dagger to a background thread" (components must be ready before use) or "remove Dagger".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are all singletons eagerly created? Is fastInit enabled? Is baseline profile in use? What is in the 310 ms by class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Defer non-critical initialization out of Application.onCreate (run after first frame).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) eager construction of heavy scoped objects while building the component; (b) class loading of many factory classes without a baseline profile; (c) the new SDK (40 ms, minor).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto/Systrace with custom trace sections around heavy providers; Android Studio profiler method trace; compare with -Adagger.fastInit=enabled build (verify effect); check baseline profile coverage for generated classes.
  5. Root cause: Large main-thread init of eager singletons (HTTP client, DB, crash SDK) plus class-load cost across hundreds of factories.
  6. Fix: Short-term: make heavy singletons Lazy/Provider at the injection site; move non-essential init to a startup scheduler. Mid-term: enable fast init; add generated factory classes to baseline profile via macrobenchmark generation. Long-term: split graph so screen-specific bindings are in subcomponents created later.
class App : Application() {
    @Inject lateinit var heavy: Lazy<HeavySdk>
    override fun onCreate() { super.onCreate(); component.inject(this); /* no heavy.get() here */ }
}
  1. Prevention: Startup benchmark in CI (macrobenchmark) with a regression threshold; trace sections around component creation.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not initialize the component off main without guaranteeing readiness (race); not drop DI; fast init has measurable trade-offs, test it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lazy moves the cost into the first screen? → Yes: choose what is on the critical path; prefetch off the main thread after first frame.
  • Baseline profile helps how? → Precompiles hot paths, reducing class-load and JIT cost; verify gains by measurement.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: 70% of the cost was three eagerly built SDK wrappers nobody needed before the first screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Dagger.
  • Hire: Lazy providers, defers init, measures with trace.
  • Strong hire: fast init, baseline profiles, subcomponent splitting, CI benchmark.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test code that uses Dagger, and when do you build a test component versus constructing objects by hand?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand DI's testing benefits and avoid framework-heavy unit tests.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unit tests construct the class directly with fakes: no Dagger at all. That is the main benefit of constructor injection. Dagger shows up in integration or instrumented tests, where I create a test component that swaps real modules for fake modules, and in a few graph-validation tests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Layers: (1) unit: Foo(fakeRepo); (2) integration of a subgraph: a test @Component including real modules for most things and fake modules for network/clock/dispatchers; (3) instrumented UI: replace the component with a test one in a custom Application/test runner. Dagger forbids overriding a binding by simply adding another module in the same component (duplicate error), so the test component must exclude the production module and include the fake one, or the production module must be structured so the replaced binding lives in a swappable module. Inject dispatchers and clocks so tests are deterministic.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Singleton
@Component(modules = [FakeNetworkModule::class, RepoModule::class])
interface TestAppComponent : AppComponent {
    @Component.Factory interface Factory { fun create(@BindsInstance app: Application): TestAppComponent }
}
@Module object FakeNetworkModule { @Provides @Singleton fun api(): Api = FakeApi() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Building a Dagger component inside every unit test; slow and unnecessary.
  • Test module cannot override because production module is included: duplicate binding.
  • Sharing a mutable fake across tests via a singleton component.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does Hilt simplify this? → @TestInstallIn replaces modules automatically (see the Hilt chunk).
  2. Test a module itself? → Rarely; test the behavior it wires, or validate the graph builds.
  3. Flaky tests from DI? → Shared scoped state across tests; recreate the component per test.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use Mockito with Dagger". Senior: direct construction first, minimal component layers, swappable module boundaries, fresh component per test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An instrumented suite flaked until each test built its own component; a leftover singleton cache was carrying state between tests.

questions.contextHtml: A 45-module app splits :feature:orders:api and :feature:orders:impl. The orders team wants to own their Dagger module and keep impl invisible. Today :app lists 38 feature modules in its component, and :app build is 5 min. A new rule says feature modules must not depend on each other's impl. Checkout needs OrdersNavigator from orders; analytics needs an event sink contributed by every feature.
questions.promptHtml: Where do the bindings live, who wires what, and how do you keep it fast and boundary-safe?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Everything in :app, with impl exposed to :app and consumed anywhere. Or each feature gets its own full component with duplicated singletons.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Hilt or Dagger? Is :app the only place seeing all impl modules? Are features ever dynamic-delivered?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None: design question; prototype with orders.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) api holds interfaces; impl holds a @Module with @Binds Interface -> Impl plus @InstallIn/component listing; :app depends on impl only as a runtime wiring edge; (b) component dependencies per feature with exposed contracts; (c) everything in :app.
  4. How I'd verify each: Module graph report to confirm no impl -> impl edges; compile times; a trial removal of an impl from :app to see only wiring errors.
  5. Root cause of risk: Wiring needs a place that sees impl: the composition root; this is unavoidable but should contain no logic.
  6. Fix: Option (a): impl exposes its module; :app includes it; consumers inject OrdersNavigator from api. Event sinks via @IntoSet multibinding of AnalyticsContributor.
// :feature:orders:impl
@Module interface OrdersModule { @Binds fun nav(i: OrdersNavigatorImpl): OrdersNavigator }
// :app
@Component(modules = [OrdersModule::class, /* other impl modules */]) interface AppComponent
  1. Prevention: Gradle dependency rules or a convention plugin that fails if impl is a dependency of anything but :app; Konsist test; module graph checked in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: :app knows all impl modules, so it recompiles when wiring changes, a price for boundary clarity; not per-feature components with duplicated infrastructure; not expose impl via api configuration.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compile time of :app growing? → Make impl dependencies runtimeOnly where possible, wiring through a small generated aggregation module; measure first.
  • Dynamic feature module? → Needs its own component or entry-point-based discovery, since :app cannot compile against it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "just reference impl once" shortcut spread to 12 modules in a quarter; a dependency-rule check in CI stopped the next 20.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: everything in :app, no boundary rules.
  • Hire: api/impl binding module with composition root wiring and multibinding.
  • Strong hire: enforcement via tooling, build cost reasoning, and dynamic module caveat.
